legend: It is a sunny day on Columbia campus, and Alice and Bob decide to go to Butler Lawns to play their favorite game: Permutation Game. Since the weather is so nice, Alice wants to stay on the lawns as long as possible, while Bob has a midterm the next day and wants to get home to study.
Permutation Game is played as follows:
Alice receives a permutation a%%ZSMJ0%% and Bob receives a permutation b%%ZSMJ1%%, both of size n%%ZSMJ2%%∗%%ZSMJ3%%.
Alice chooses an index i%%ZSMJ4%% (1≤i≤n%%ZSMJ5%%) and places a token on position i%%ZSMJ6%% of her permutation a%%ZSMJ7%%.
Bob, after seeing where Alice has placed her token, chooses an index j%%ZSMJ8%% (1≤j≤n%%ZSMJ9%%) and places his own token on position j%%ZSMJ10%% of his permutation b%%ZSMJ11%%.
Alice and Bob each follow their permutation one step at a time:   Alice moves her token to index ai%%ZSMJ12%%, then aai%%ZSMJ13%%, and so on.
Bob moves his token to index bj%%ZSMJ14%%, then bbj%%ZSMJ15%%, and so on.

∗%%ZSMJ16%%A permutation of length n%%ZSMJ17%% is an array consisting of n%%ZSMJ18%% distinct integers from 1%%ZSMJ19%% to n%%ZSMJ20%% in arbitrary order. For example, [2%%ZSMJ21%%, 3%%ZSMJ22%%, 1%%ZSMJ23%%, 5%%ZSMJ24%%, 4%%ZSMJ25%%] is a permutation, but [1%%ZSMJ26%%, 2%%ZSMJ27%%, 2%%ZSMJ28%%] is not a permutation (2%%ZSMJ29%% appears twice in the array), and [1%%ZSMJ30%%, 3%%ZSMJ31%%, 4%%ZSMJ32%%] is also not a permutation (n=3%%ZSMJ33%% but there is a 4%%ZSMJ34%% in the array).
input: The first line of input contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ35%% (1≤n≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ36%%).
The second line of input contains n%%ZSMJ37%% distinct integers a1,a2,...,an%%ZSMJ38%% — Alice's permutation a%%ZSMJ39%%.
The third line of input contains n%%ZSMJ40%% distinct integers b1,b2,...,bn%%ZSMJ41%% — Bob's permutation b%%ZSMJ42%%.
output: Output a single integer — the number of steps that will be performed in the game, assuming both players play optimally.
note: In the first sample, regardless of which indices Alice and Bob place their tokens on to start, the process will last for just one step.

In the second example, Alice may place her token at index 3%%ZSMJ43%%, and Bob, seeing where Alice has placed her token, places his at index 1%%ZSMJ44%%. After one step, Alice's token will be at index 4%%ZSMJ45%% and Bob's will be at index 3%%ZSMJ46%%. After two steps, Alice's token will be at index 5%%ZSMJ47%% and Bob's will be at 5%%ZSMJ48%%. And after three steps, Alice's token returns to index 3%%ZSMJ49%%, while Bob's returns to index 1%%ZSMJ50%%.
